claims.text: Controlled isothermal aging of a single-phase, homogeneous magnetic HEA will induce nanoscale precipitate formation or phase separation.
The aging-induced nanoscale precipitates or phase boundaries will act as domain-wall pinning centers.
Pinning by the precipitates will impede domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal.
Impeded domain-wall motion will require a larger applied field to reverse magnetization, thereby increasing coercivity.
The initial HEA is single-phase and chemically homogeneous.
The initial HEA has low coercivity because it lacks microstructural pinning centers.
An intermediate aging temperature can promote nanoscale decomposition while a higher annealing temperature can leave a more homogeneous matrix.
A nanoscale phase-separated aged condition can have higher coercivity than a high-temperature-aged homogeneous condition.
Controlled aging will increase coercivity relative to an otherwise identical non-aged sample.
The non-aged control will retain a uniform microstructure.
The coercivity enhancement will occur only within a suitable aging temperature and time window.
Excessively high aging temperatures may eliminate the nanoscale decomposition and reduce the coercivity enhancement.
Prolonged aging may cause microstructural coarsening that negates the coercivity enhancement.
Coercivity will be measured at room temperature with composition and baseline processing held constant between aged and non-aged samples.
The optimal aging temperature, aging time, precipitate distribution, and coercivity increase are not yet known.
Microscopy will be used to determine whether the aged samples contain nanoscale precipitates, and magnetic hysteresis measurements will quantify coercivity.
The hypothesis will be falsified if aging fails to produce nanoscale precipitates or fails to yield a statistically significant coercivity increase over the matched control.
